Dial of the twelve hours, coloured by the combination period, the sign rising in each; dots mark the nectar periods

The ring shows the combination period, the sign rising in each hour after the All-Benefiting Mirror (ཀུན་ཕན་མེ་ལོང, kun phan me long), coloured lucky where the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) says to accomplish it; dots mark Jupiter\'s nectar periods. Clock time at your place: the hours run from the hare hour at 05:00 to the tiger hour ending at 05:00 the next morning.

Inner ring: the combination period, the sign rising in each hour, coloured lucky where the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) says to accomplish it; dots mark Jupiter\'s nectar periods. Outer rings: vitality and body, coloured by their pebbles. Clock time at your place: the hours run from the hare hour at 05:00 to the tiger hour ending at 05:00 the next morning.

The hour\'s element follows from the lunar date\'s (%1$s) by the hour\'s animal: hare, monkey and ox hours take its son; dragon, bird and tiger its friend; snake and dog its enemy; horse and pig its mother; sheep and mouse the same element.

Phugpa (ཕུག་པ, phug pa) version, computed with the arithmetic of Svante Janson, “Tibetan Calendar Mathematics” (2007, revised 2014 and 2022), epoch 806, with the moon\'s daily anomaly of 1/28 used by the Men-Tsee-Khang (སྨན་རྩིས་ཁང, sman rtsis khang) almanac. Lunar mansion, yoga, karaṇa and the lunar-day cycles follow Janson §10 and Appendix E. Checked against Janson\'s table of Losar (ལོ་གསར, lo gsar) dates for 1927–2046 and, day by day, against Edward Henning\'s computed Phugpa calendars (kalacakra.org).

Tenpō rules in Japan Standard Time: months begin on the day of new moon and are numbered by the major solar term they contain. For 2033 the leap month is 閏11月, the recommended resolution of the 2033 problem. Solar terms, new moons and 雑節 are checked against the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (暦要項).

The almanac annotations (十二直, 二十八宿, 九星, 選日 and 暦注下段) follow the rules tabulated in Japanese Wikipedia after 岡田芳朗・阿久根末忠『現代こよみ読み解き事典』 (1993), and are checked day by day against こよみのページ (koyomi8.com). 神吉日 and 凶会日 are left out: their full rules are not recoverable.

Jean Meeus, “Astronomical Algorithms” (2nd ed., 1998): new moons from chapter 49, the sun from the VSOP87D series of Bretagnon and Francou, ΔT from the polynomials of Espenak and Meeus (NASA). Everything is computed on this phone; the app has no internet access.

Every reading names its source. Japanese: こよみ博物館 of the almanac publisher Todan (六曜, 十二直, 二十八宿); Japanese Wikipedia (選日, 暦注下段, 九星, 九星気学, 歳徳神, 庚申待), whose adapted text is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0; NAOJ 暦Wiki (雑節, 節句, 十三夜); the dictionaries on Kotobank. Tibetan: the translation of the hair-cutting days by Lama Zopa Rinpoche (བླ་མ་བཟོད་པ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ, bla ma bzod pa rin po che), FPMT, 2008; Edition Rabten\'s Tibetan calendar; Edward Henning\'s symbolic details of the calendar and his electional astrology of the five components (the lunar mansions and the activity lists); and the Prayer Invoking the Benefits of the Festival of the Tenth Day (ཚེས་བཅུའི་ཕན་ཡོན་གསོལ་འདེབས, tshes bcu\'i phan yon gsol \'debs) by Jigme Lingpa (འཇིགས་མེད་གླིང་པ, \'jigs med gling pa) from Lotsawa House; the colours and arrangement of the nine numbers from Alexander Berzin\'s Details of Tibetan Astrology (Study Buddhism); the four aspects and the pebbles of the day, month and year from the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) of Desi Sangye Gyatso (སྡེ་སྲིད་སངས་རྒྱས་རྒྱ་མཚོ, sde srid sangs rgyas rgya mtsho) with the Moonbeams (ཟླ་བའི་འོད་ཟེར, zla ba\'i \'od zer) of Lochen Dharmashri (ལོ་ཆེན་དྷརྨ་ཤྲཱི, lo chen d+har+ma shrI). Readings not adapted from Wikipedia are the app\'s own English summaries of the cited sources, under the app\'s licence.

Tibetan terms are written in Tibetan script from their Wylie spelling, checked against the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) of Desi Sangye Gyatso (སྡེ་སྲིད་སངས་རྒྱས་རྒྱ་མཚོ, sde srid sangs rgyas rgya mtsho); their pronunciation follows the THL Simplified Phonetic Transcription of Standard Tibetan (David Germano and Nicolas Tournadre, 2003).

Shown, not weighed. The White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) calls a person\'s own weekdays and mansions of particular importance, but neither it nor any other text found places them against the combination of weekday and mansion; the day\'s tone and its lists stand as weighed above.

Every work to avoid, for you
“On the enemy weekday (དགྲ་གཟའ, dgra gza\') of one\'s element every work is to be avoided”: the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po), vol. 2, p. 338.

“On the death mansion (འཆི་བའི་སྐར་མ, \'chi ba\'i skar ma) anything is bad”: the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po), vol. 2, p. 338. Your slayer mansion (གཤེད་སྐར, gshed skar) is the death mansion.

The White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) makes the enemy weekday and the death mansion absolute for you, so the brief gives you no list of good works today; the day\'s tone, its works to avoid and its hours stand as weighed above. Your other days are shown, not weighed: no text found places them against the combination of weekday and mansion.

Within its hour the combination period, the sign then rising, outweighs every factor of the day: the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) holds the work of planet, mansion, karaṇa and yoga complete in its house (vol. 2, p. 376). What its reading names good or to avoid stands above the day\'s lists while the hour lasts. The nectar periods are shown, not weighed. Tap a time to open its hour.

Decides the day\'s tone in the brief today.
The tone is the day\'s for its works; it does not weigh the merit of the festival or observance.

Weighed as the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) and the All-Benefiting Mirror (ཀུན་ཕན་མེ་ལོང, kun phan me long) say, by one rule for the day and for each work. Where the named combination of weekday and mansion and the element pair agree, the combination is the day\'s result, and what any other factor says against it is outweighed, even where the weekday and the mansion agree; it decides a work only where the element pair names it, so a lucky day keeps the date\'s and the weekday\'s prohibitions. Where the two disagree, and for every other work, the strongest factor that takes a side decides, in this order: Rāhu, the weekday, the mansion, the special days of weekday and mansion (one voice, and none when they disagree), the date, the karaṇa, the yoga and the day animal. The White Beryl weighs mixed factors by their strength, not by their number. Rāhu, the mansion and the day animal have no tone of their own and decide only the works they name; the trigram decides only works no other factor names. Outweighed factors are not shown.

One voice in the weighing: the named combination of weekday and mansion and its element pair. Where the two agree, the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) makes the combination the day\'s result, outweighing every other factor, even a good weekday and mansion (vol. 2, p. 333); where they disagree it has no tone, and the strongest factor that takes a side decides the day.

The days are ordered by the strength the texts give. First those on which the combination of weekday and mansion makes the work good: the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) makes it the result even where the planet and the mansion are each good (vol. 2, p. 333). Then by the strongest factor naming the work good, in the order of vol. 2, p. 376: Rāhu, the weekday, the mansion, the special days, the lunar date, the karaṇa, the yoga, the day animal, the trigram; within one rank a day whose combination is lucky comes first. Past that the order is the app\'s own: the sum of the weights of the factors on the work\'s side, ten for the combination down to one for the trigram, then the earlier day. Each day is weighed as its own page weighs it; a day no factor names is blank, not neutral.

The combination period follows the month and the hour only, so every day of a Tibetan month has the same hours (the All-Benefiting Mirror (ཀུན་ཕན་མེ་ལོང, kun phan me long), §9); the reading of the sign then rising names the work good or to avoid (the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po), vol. 2, pp. 371–376), and where the White Beryl\'s chapter on the works names the work\'s own signs, they come first, as its particular case (pp. 385–428). The hours say when within a day, never which day: a day to avoid is not offered for its good hours.

A ring marks your enemy weekday or your death mansion: on them the White Beryl (བཻཌཱུར་དཀར་པོ, bai DUr dkar po) avoids every work (vol. 2, p. 338), so they are not offered. Your other days are marked and not weighed.
